newsitem.title: FRANCE: French cities under pollution alert for second day.
newsitem.headline: French cities under pollution alert for second day.

text.p: Paris police lowered speed limits and urged drivers to leave their cars at home on Wednesday as the French capital tried to cut car emissions to prevent a pollution crisis during a summer heat wave.

Air quality was still poor after officials in Paris, Lille, Lyon and Strasbourg issued an air pollution alert on Tuesday as a combination of heat, sunlight, car exhaust fumes and a lack of wind pushed pollution to health-threatening levels.
Public health officials have urged the elderly, small children and people with respiratory problems to limit their physical activity during the alert.

Pollution levels were measured at "level two," the midpoint on the official scale and one step below the "level three" alert that would require curbs on private cars and free public transport in the large cities.
Speed limits were lowered by 20 km per hour in Paris and drivers in the city were urged to accelerate slowly and to switch off car engines when stationary.
Paris authorities offered free parking in residential areas to persuade commuters to leave their cars behind, while Strasbourg laid on extra buses and trams.

Slight northwest winds cut pollution levels in the capital in the afternoon, but the Paris pollution monitoring authority Airparif said the alerts could continue for the next few days as midday temperatures hover above 30 degrees centigrade.
Lyon registered high levels of ozone pollution, caused by car exhaust fumes, and sulphur dioxide from factories.
The Greens, a partner in the ruling left-wing coalition, urged authorities to curb car traffic in major cities.
The pollution alert has also triggered a debate about environmental policy between the new Socialist government and the former conservative administration.

Corinne Lepage, the former environment minister, said she hoped her leftist successor, Greens leader Dominique Voynet, would "have the political courage" to restrict private cars, even though level three had not been reached.
Lepage wants to allow private cars only on alternate days, according to the numbers on their licence plates.
But the Environment Ministry did not opt for such limits, promising instead a long-term change in transport policy with a "green vignette" allowing low-polluting cars on the roads.
Cars that failed a clean exhaust test would be barred from the roads during a pollution alert.
"Dominique Voynet considers this system more educational," a ministry spokesman said, adding that a decree to this effect would be issued later this year.
